quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Bonus workshops you can join only if you feel like it.
quests.explanation: 'Mandatory' is a formal twin of compulsory, and 'elective' is the school word for subjects you choose.
quests.textToSpeak: At our school, swimming lessons are *compulsory* for every pupil in the first two years.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Whom does everyone ask for advice on the subject?
quests.explanation: 'Pro' is the casual version of this word, while 'novice' is the formal synonym of beginner.
quests.textToSpeak: Five years ago she was a *beginner*, yet now she competes internationally.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: What does an apprentice in a workshop get that a textbook can't give?
quests.explanation: The noun is spelled 'practice' in both varieties, but only British English spells the verb 'practise'.
quests.textToSpeak: We spent the whole first term on *theory* and never touched the lab equipment.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Who receives the monthly salary?
quests.explanation: The endings show the roles: -er does the action, -ee receives it. Compare trainer/trainee and interviewer/interviewee.
quests.textToSpeak: Under the new law, every *employer* must provide a safe workplace and proper training.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Which kind of job fits around university lectures?
quests.explanation: Before a noun it is hyphenated (a part-time job); after a verb it acts as an adverb (she works part time).
quests.textToSpeak: Since he works *full-time* at the hospital, he only has evenings free for classes.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: She loses her title and moves to a smaller role after a big mistake.
quests.explanation: 'Demote' sounds harsh and is rare in speech; people usually say 'lose their position'.
quests.textToSpeak: After five years of excellent results, the company finally decided to *promote* her.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Paperwork that never changes and nobody chases.
quests.explanation: Hospitals and inboxes use 'non-urgent' as the plain negative.
quests.textToSpeak: This is an *urgent* request, so please reply within the hour.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Someone who has never worked for the company is this kind of applicant.
quests.explanation: Adverts often say 'internal applicants only' or 'open to external candidates'.
quests.textToSpeak: Please don't share this link: the vacancy is open to *internal* candidates only.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: She joins the call from her kitchen table, so she works this way.
quests.explanation: 'Hybrid' means a mix of both, and 'working from home' is the casual phrase.
quests.textToSpeak: Unlike the sales staff, our support team works *on-site*, at the head office.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: He doubled the price once he noticed you were a tourist.
quests.explanation: 'Overpriced' is the matching adjective: the jacket was overpriced, the deal a rip-off.
quests.textToSpeak: Considering I paid next to nothing, I thought the jacket was a *bargain*.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Phone companies spread the cost over many months.
quests.explanation: Americans write 'installments' with a double l; British English uses 'instalments'.
quests.textToSpeak: To get the discount, you'd have to pay *upfront* for the whole year.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Prices on a high-street shelf are called this.
quests.explanation: Wholesale prices are lower per item because buyers order in large quantities.
quests.textToSpeak: Unlike most chains, this company buys *wholesale* and then sells direct to customers online.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Flights that need border control and a passport.
quests.explanation: In business it also means inside a country's own market: domestic sales.
quests.textToSpeak: Since it's only a *domestic* flight, nobody will ask to see your passport.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: On the day you go home, the key card goes back to the front desk.
quests.explanation: As nouns they fuse into one word: check-in, checkout. Hotels and airports use both.
quests.textToSpeak: The hotel says guests can *check in* after two, but the room may be ready earlier.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: You contact the airline to undo the reservation.
quests.explanation: The past tense is 'cancelled' in British English and 'canceled' in American English.
quests.textToSpeak: Before prices go up, we should *book* the hotel for the whole week.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Where you sit if you pick the cheapest ticket and the smallest seat.
quests.explanation: Business class sits in between, and Americans also call economy 'coach'.
quests.textToSpeak: On long trips, she treats herself and always flies *first class*.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Which seat lets you stretch your legs without disturbing anyone?
quests.explanation: In a row of three, the seat between them is the middle seat, which nobody chooses.
quests.textToSpeak: On daytime flights, I always request a *window* seat.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: What goes onto the conveyor belt at the desk and comes back at the carousel?
quests.explanation: British English often says hand luggage and hold luggage.
quests.textToSpeak: You can bring one *carry-on* bag into the cabin without paying extra.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: You have a package for a friend and stop by her door.
quests.explanation: Pronouns go in the middle: pick it up, drop them off.
quests.textToSpeak: On your way home, could you *pick up* the parcel from the post office?

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: That sign vanishes from the lift door when the technician finishes.
quests.explanation: 'Operational' is the formal word, and 'in service' is used for transport.
quests.textToSpeak: The ticket machine is *out of order*, so pay the driver.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: What a diner says to the chef about a wonderful meal.
quests.explanation: Complaint has an 'a' like 'annoyed'; compliment has an 'i' like 'nice'.
quests.textToSpeak: By morning, the hotel had received a *complaint* about the noise from the floor above.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: What do your ears do while someone else has the floor?
quests.explanation: With people, talk and listen both take 'to'. 'Hear' is different, since you can hear without trying.
quests.textToSpeak: Let me *talk* first, and then it's your turn to ask questions.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: What do you ask a soft-spoken person to do on a bad line?
quests.explanation: No single word captures it: 'speak up' means louder, while 'speak clearly' means easier to understand.
quests.textToSpeak: Sorry, I didn't catch that — you *mumble* a little.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: In a language test, which part happens with an examiner and a microphone?
quests.explanation: 'Verbal' can mean spoken or word-based, so it's a bit ambiguous, and 'oral' is clearer.
quests.textToSpeak: At this university, half of your final grade depends on a *written* exam.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Before checking your stomach, a doctor asks you to do this.
quests.explanation: 'Lie' (lie, lay, lain) and 'lay' (to put down) confuse even native speakers.
quests.textToSpeak: It's time to *get up* — the bus leaves in twenty minutes.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: A relaxed friend says this when you apologise for being slow.
quests.explanation: 'No rush' is the friendly, everyday way to say the same thing.
quests.textToSpeak: *Hurry up* — the film starts in five minutes!

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: At day's end they do this before heading to the car park.
quests.explanation: 'Clock out' comes from old time clocks that punched a card, and many workplaces still say it.
quests.textToSpeak: Every morning, warehouse staff have to *clock in* before their shift begins.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Prefer the café to the classroom, and you do this to the lesson.
quests.explanation: 'Skip' is informal, 'miss' is neutral, and Americans also say 'cut class'.
quests.textToSpeak: To qualify for the exam, students must *attend* at least eighty percent of classes.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Harsh reviewers do this to a film they dislike.
quests.explanation: Constructive criticism is meant to help, so the word isn't always negative.
quests.textToSpeak: The teacher always finds a way to *praise* even weak work.

quests.instruction: Speak the opposite of the highlighted word.
quests.hint: Which paragraph does the reader reach last?
quests.explanation: A conclusion sums things up and shouldn't add new ideas.
quests.textToSpeak: Your arguments are good, but this essay needs a stronger *introduction*.
